parsed.explanation: No law criminalises trans identity or expression, same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 1993, and gender identity is a protected ground for hate-crime aggravation (2017) with police guidance (2019) requiring officers to address trans detainees by identified gender, plus several hundred officials trained. Nothing in the dossier documents visitor-facing border, document, facility or custody exposure — the resident LGR surgery requirement is not a traveller rule. The offsetting weakness is tier-3: documented societal hostility with thin recourse, police disregarding anti-LGBT complaints, attacks unpunished. But the violence record is dated (2001, 2009, 2014; none since) and the prevalence surveys are LGBT-wide and stale, so neither carries current weight. Formal machinery part-operates; enforcement does not reliably. Reduced-risk tier, below jurisdictions with working remedies.

entry_documents.exposure: Not documented. No reported border friction, marker scrutiny, or refusal of entry for trans visitors; a travel-community note mentions residual 'immoral sexual needs' provisions but no use against trans travellers is recorded.
entry_documents.protection: Not documented for visitors specifically; no trans-specific entry restriction on the books.
entry_documents.interaction: Visitor documents are home-issued; the dossier documents no mechanism linking them to domestic gender-recognition processes.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: A detained transgender woman was assaulted by an officer (reported 2019); activists say complaints of anti-LGBT hate crimes are disregarded and attacks often go unpunished.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Police guidelines require officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of ID documents; 500+ officers, prosecutors and judges trained on the 2017 hate-crime provisions.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Training and guidelines exist but the dossier shows enforcement gaps; the guideline's current status after 2019 is unsourced.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Not documented. No facility-access, ward-placement or custody-assignment rule reaching trans visitors is described.

care_services.exposure: Not documented for visitors. No refusal of care, medication seizure or insurance exclusion is recorded.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Culture is strongly heteronormative and ostracism and harassment persist; no state threat-framing or criminalisation of gender expression exists.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Gender identity is a protected ground in hate-crime and hate-speech law (2015 code, in force 2017); discrimination barred in the Penal Code and Labour Code; LGBT groups can register.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Paper protection with weak operational follow-through; no comprehensive equality statute.

minors_guardians.exposure: Not documented for travelling minors. A 2019 figure (79% of LGBT-identified young people reporting bullying or ostracism) is LGBT-wide, not trans-specific, and not a visitor measure.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Trans-specific violence documented: 2009 kidnapping, beating and sexual assault of three trans women by a hyper-nationalist group, unreported to police; other recorded attacks in 2001 and 2014, the most recent in this record.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Hate-crime aggravation for gender-identity motive; police training; no evidence of prosecution in the recorded cases.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Under-reporting driven by fear of victimisation meets documented police disinclination to pursue hate-crime complaints, so the aggravator rarely operates.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Remedies described as not taken seriously; attacks often result in no punishment.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Hate-crime statute, training programme, police gender-address guideline, registrable advocacy organisations.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Whether conditions differ outside the capital, and whether the 2019 police guidance still operates, are unresolved; whether any comprehensive equality law was enacted after 2014 is unresolved.

anchor_checks.comparison: 0.35-A has a state-run register barring trans visitors at the border, enforced routinely with no effective remedy. Here there is no entry-side exclusion at all; the exposure is societal hostility and weak police follow-through, not state admission control. This dossier sits materially higher.

0.55-B routes trans travellers into extended secondary screening with discretionary refusal and administrative return. Here no such screening practice is documented; entry is unremarkable. The 0.55-B exposure is traveller-facing and institutional, so this dossier is comparable or slightly better, offset by its documented unpunished violence.

0.75-C combines trained border officers with a civil-liberties tribunal granting written reasons and compensation, and detention is brief. This dossier has training and a hate-crime statute but explicitly no working remedy — complaints disregarded, attacks unpunished — so it sits clearly below 0.75-C.

parsed.synthesis: The operative regime is one of formal protection without reliable enforcement. A trans visitor faces no criminalisation, no documented border or document friction, no facility or custody rule keyed to birth sex, and gender identity is an aggravating ground in hate-crime law backed by police training and a guideline on addressing detainees by identified gender. What subtracts is tier-3 societal hostility with thin recourse: documented anti-trans violence, under-reporting, and police said to disregard such complaints. That record is dated however — no incident since 2014 — and the prevalence surveys are stale and LGBT-wide, so it cannot carry current weight. Dateability of both the good and the bad facts is the central uncertainty; the score reflects law and institutions partly aligned with acceptance in principle, eroding in practice.
